problem: Existing VLM-based zero-shot object navigation grounds targets passively from whatever viewpoint is incidentally seen during exploration, and makes a one-shot binary decision from the current observation. This causes premature or wrong grounding under occlusion, bad distance, and ambiguous or distractor objects, especially for free-form descriptions with attributes and spatial relations.
motivation: Real users give open-ended instructions such as 'my black bag on the red stool next to the trash can', which need compositional grounding that CLIP-style models handle poorly. VLMs are trained on static third-person images, so egocentric partial views hurt them. Humans move to get a better view and remember uncertain candidates for later, which motivates active viewpoint selection and memory replay.
key_idea: Wrap an off-the-shelf VLM in a grounding loop that re-observes candidate targets from an optimized viewpoint before accepting them and, if exploration fails, replays stored keyframes to pick the target.
insight: Grounding quality depends on input quality as much as on the VLM: the ablation shows that removing active grounding or memory replay each drops SR from 0.405 to about 0.31, so both matter. Feeding the raw RGB alongside the annotated image also helps (SR 0.263 without raw vs 0.285 with). Single-view grounding is the bottleneck of the VLN-Game baseline.
method: Visual semantic perception: an open-vocabulary detector (Grounding DINO) takes target and landmark names from the LLM-parsed instruction, SAM produces masks, and CLIP features and back-projected point clouds build a ConceptGraphs-style 3D object memory.
Visual memory: keyframes are stored as pairs of raw RGB and an annotated image with numbered bounding boxes, and a frame becomes a keyframe when it introduces a new target object.
VLM initial grounding: GPT-4o receives the annotated and raw images plus the instruction and outputs the index of the matching box, or false.

Active grounding by viewpoint optimization: after a positive initial grounding, a genetic algorithm (DEAP) on the 2D grid minimizes -R_visible -R_fov + P_distance + P_feasibility. The robot navigates to the resulting viewpoint and re-grounds, and the target is accepted only if both rounds agree.

Memory-based reserved grounding: if exploration ends without a confirmed target, up to 13 keyframes are uniformly sampled from visual memory and the VLM picks an image and a box, whose 3D position comes from object memory.
Exploration and navigation: frontier-based exploration on VLN-Game-style similarity semantic maps, Fast Marching Method for long-term goal planning, and greedy discrete actions.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for grounding; Grounding DINO, SAM and CLIP as frozen perception modules
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (480x640) plus odometry, and a language description
setting.action_space: discrete MOVE FORWARD, TURN LEFT, TURN RIGHT, LOOK UP, LOOK DOWN, STOP (Habitat); real robot uses A* plus MPC

numbers_note: Metrics were printed as fractions (0.408) and converted to percent for SR and SPL. Only the GOAT-Bench language-goal subset is evaluated. Real-world experiments are qualitative only.
results: MAG-Nav reaches SR 0.408, SPL 0.156 and DTG 4.027 on the GOAT-Bench language instructions, beating VLN-Game with GPT-4o (0.367 / 0.132 / 4.093), CoW (0.285) and LLM2CLIP (0.313). Ablations show that removing active grounding or memory replay drops SR to about 0.31. Real-world qualitative tests on a Go2 quadruped succeeded at rejecting distractors and recalling previously seen objects.
limitations: GPT-4o grounding adds latency, which may limit real-time use.
Evaluation covers only one benchmark subset, and the real-world tests are only a few qualitative tasks with no quantitative results.
Absolute SR stays around 41%, and SPL gains are small because of the extra viewpoint detours.
